title: Swinging a sword WON'T make you jacked
summary: NH explains why the Guts-inspired trend of swinging a heavy sword to get big fails: the movement patterns barely hit the target muscles, repetitive heavy swings cause overuse injuries, momentum removes the negative, and a fixed-weight implement allows no progressive overload. He notes that medieval knights did resistance training too, and releases a free 3-day full-body Knight program with sword practice and conditioning days.
claims: The sword-for-gains trend comes from it being cool to men and from imitating Guts in Berserk
Sword swinging fails for hypertrophy for three reasons: poor biomechanics, overuse from repeating one plane of motion, and no progressive overload
The overhead swing people copy is mostly a front raise followed by a pullover pattern, so it mainly hits shoulders, traps and upper back; most people don't step in, so legs are left out
Horizontal swings are mostly core rotation, and studies on the similar golf swing show underhand swings are mostly lower body (quads, adductors)
Sword swinging ignores the chest entirely and barely trains biceps, the very muscles people admire on Guts
Bodybuilding programs use several movement patterns per muscle partly to avoid overuse injuries from always loading the same axis
Benching three times a week as your only press can bring shoulder and biceps tendon pain, not because the lift is dangerous but because of repetition
Practice implements are deliberately light: kendo shinai 300-500 g, fencing practice weapons about 500 g, because moving heavy objects fast causes tendon problems
Replica giant swords weigh at least 5 kg, about five times heavier than kendo practice tools, enough to cause overuse injuries; Guts' sword would be 150-180 kg
A sword's weight sits far from the hands, creating a long lever arm and momentum, so the exercise becomes about controlling inertia rather than loading muscle

Lifters standardized on barbells, dumbbells, machines and cables because they make load predictable and correct the strength curve; the more technique an implement demands, the less hypertrophy you get
The negative is a key part of the rep for hypertrophy; with a sword, momentum removes it, so you get roughly half a rep
A fixed-weight implement leaves only more reps, more sets, shorter rest or slower tempo for overload, none of which matches adding weight
Progressive overload is more than adding weight, but to keep growing you eventually have to get stronger and lift more
Adding plates to a sword like Guts does only worsens balance and momentum
Medieval knights did resistance training: squires from age 10 carried armor, they threw stones, ran in armor, did weighted pull-ups on ladders, overhead presses and push-ups
Lifting weights on the side also makes you better at swinging a sword
Knight program: 3 full-body days (Mon, Wed, Fri), sword practice Tue and Sat, conditioning (rucking, swimming or rock climbing) Thu and Sun
Sword practice twice a week is enough so gym work can feed sword progress; daily swinging gives worse results

FB1: weighted pull-ups 3x3-5 + one-arm military press 3x8-12; Zercher good morning 3x6-10 + Russian twists 3x10-15; weighted push-ups 3x6-10 + preacher curls 3x8-12; walking lunges 3x30 m + Y raises 3x10-15
FB2: Zercher squats 3x6-10 + upright rows 3x10-15; Kroc rows 3x8-12 + triceps extension 3x10-15; KB swing 3x10-15 + spider curls 3x8-12; floor press 3x6-10 + cable finger curls 3x10-15
FB3: weighted dips 3x3-5 + decline sit-ups 3x8-12; farmer carry 3x30 m + landmine press 3x6-10; weighted chin-ups 3x4-8 + face pulls 3x10-15; leg press 3x10-15 + hammer curls 3x6-10
He also offers a separate free Guts physique program for those who only care about the look
